newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary NATO envoy accuses Russia of Cold War pose.
newsitem.headline: Hungary NATO envoy accuses Russia of Cold War pose.

text.p: Hungary's ambassador to NATO accused Russia on Monday of using the language of the Cold War in renewing its calls for the alliance to abandon its plans to expand eastwards.
"When messages like that come out people will start saying, 'Hey does that not sound familiar?'," ambassador Andras Simonyi told students at Budapest's International Business School.

Simonyi was responding to Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's speech earlier on Monday in which he told leaders from more than 50 nations that Moscow firmly opposed NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

"We have declared clearly, and declare clearly now, our firm opposition to the North Atlantic alliance's plans to move itself and its military infrastructure towards our territory," he told the Lisbon meeting of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"Is it not clear that the appearance of new dividing lines would lead to a worsening of the whole geopolitical situation in the world?," he added
Simonyi said Hungary's logic in joining NATO stemmed from painful memories of Russia's dominant historical role in Central Europe.

"What we are doing (in applying to join NATO) is because we have a memory of 1956, the Czechs have a memory of 1968, the Poles have a memory of 1980," said Simonyi, referring to the suppression of anti-Soviet popular movements during the era of the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact.
"Even if these words do come out of Russia we will not buy it," he added. "We will stick to the logic that we have adopted."
Chernomyrdin's comments continued the tough line against NATO enlargement which he, Yeltsin and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov have taken particularly in the past few days against NATO expansion.
Simonyi said he regretted the apparent hardening of Russia's attiutude.
"I'm not very happy that cold and cold is coming out of Russia because when they were blowing hot and cold we were able to carry on a fruitful discussion with Moscow," he said.
"You don't ignore those statements but NATO has to redouble its efforts to show that we will not abandon our course."

NATO has made clear it will not go back on its plans, and a row over expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation could overshadow the OSCE summit, just as it did the organisation's last summit in Budapest in 1994.
